atoms.span: NaNoGenMo (National Novel Generation Month) is an annual programming challenge
managed by maintainers like Darius Kazemi and Hugo van Kemenade
Write and run code between November 1 (12:01 am GMT) and December 1 (12:01 am GMT) to output a text work of 50,000+ words.
Participants share both the generated text and the source code at the end of the event.
Created as a playful programming spoof of NaNoWriMo (National Novel Writing Month)

mt: 'NANOGENMO' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE EVENT, ITS PERIOD AND ITS RULE AT THEIR GRAIN; THE NOVEL FROM PROJECT GUTENBERG REPLACED BY TECHNIQUES; A COPYRIGHT REQUEST LEFT TO THE PARTICIPANT GIVEN AS A RULE
d: THE EVENT, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'NaNoGenMo (National Novel Generation Month) is an annual programming challenge where participants spend the month of November writing computer code to procedurally generate a novel of 50,000 or more words.' The core goal and rules (the period to the minute; 'Definition of a Novel: The definition is flexible'; 'Respect for copyright applies.'; sharing text and code; joining by a GitHub issue); background (a 'playful programming spoof of NaNoWriMo'; edition repositories 'spanning from 2013 onward, managed by maintainers like Darius Kazemi and Hugo van Kemenade'); an offer on participating or on techniques. Six cards: the NaNoGenMo site, Reddit, GitHub, Liza Daly, centerconsulting.com, a YouTube video; the paste ends on the video card.
reading: The innocent reading first. Asked for the event by its acronym, the Overview gives its goal, period, rules, how to join, its origin and who runs it, mainly from the event's own page, on the first day of the period the page states.
findings: THE EVENT AT ITS GRAIN. 'between November 1 (12:01 am GMT) and December 1 (12:01 am GMT)' agrees with 'This activity starts at 12:01am GMT on Nov 1st and ends at 12:01am GMT Dec 1st.'; 'Participants share both the generated text and the source code at the end of the event.' with 'The only rule is that you share at least one novel and also your source code at the end.'; joining 'by opening and updating an issue' with 'Open an issue on the edition's repo and declare your intent to participate.' The admins, '@dariusk and @hugovk' on the page, are given as 'Darius Kazemi and Hugo van Kemenade'; the first name is on the page ('based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted on a whim'), the second on no saved page.

THE NOVEL DEFINED, ITS EXAMPLES REPLACED. The page: 'The "novel" is defined however you want. It could be 50,000 repetitions of the word "meow". It could literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg.' The composition: 'traditional procedural text, Markov chains, simulations, data mashups, or creative formatting (such as guides, collections, or repeated structures)'. The novel taken whole from an existing text, the census row's ground for what the event 'makes' and how it stands to the layer, is absent; 'data mashups' is the nearest term. The resources the page points to, 'libraries, corpuses, APIs, techniques' in a per-edition issue and 'corpora , a repository of public domain lists of things', are not carried; the closing offers 'generation techniques (like Markov chains or template engines)'.

COPYRIGHT AND CREDIT. 'Respect for copyright applies.' The page asks and declines to enforce: 'Please try to respect copyright. We're not going to police it, as ultimately it's on your head if you want to just copy/paste a Stephen King novel or whatever'. The composition gives the request as a rule in force. 'The source code does not have to be licensed in a particular way' is not carried. The census row reads crediting of the generated text and its sources as left to each participant; the composition names no participant and no novel, and only the Liza Daly card's snippet begins a list of entries ('Selected Entries: B-9 Indifferenc...').

THE EDITIONS ON THE FIRST DAY. 'annual edition repositories spanning from 2013 onward' agrees with 'Editions 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021 2020 2019 2018 2017 2016 2015 2014 2013'. The run is dated 1 November 2026, the first day of the period; the census row records that the saved page 'lists no 2026 edition', and the composition names no current edition, asking 'Are you planning to participate in an upcoming NaNoGenMo'. The GitHub card's 'Oct 9, 2025' is the latest date it shows. 'spoof' is the centerconsulting card's word ('A spoof of National Novel Writing Month'); the page's is 'in the spirit of National Novel Writing Month 's interesting definition of a novel'. The sister events ('NaPoGenMo : National Poetry Generation Month' and the rest) are not carried.
analysis: The event composed at its grain from its own page, its period and its sharing rule exact. The Project Gutenberg example that marks a generated novel as made from existing text is replaced by a list of techniques, and the page's unpoliced copyright request is given as a rule.
per_note: Darius Kazemi and Hugo van Kemenade named; no institution; the event's page and its GitHub organisation carded.

evidence.record_quote: The only rule is that you share at least one novel and also your source code at the end.
The source code does not have to be licensed in a particular way, so long as you share it. The code itself does not need to be on GitHub, either.
The "novel" is defined however you want. It could be 50,000 repetitions of the word "meow". It could literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg.
Please try to respect copyright. We're not going to police it, as ultimately it's on your head if you want to just copy/paste a Stephen King novel or whatever
